argument: When risk is continuously distributed, most cases may arise from the large population at ordinary or moderately elevated risk rather than the small high-risk tail. Population-wide shifts can therefore produce more aggregate prevention even though each individual benefits only slightly.
boundary: Population strategies can expose many people to small costs or harms.
High-risk strategies may be preferable when interventions are expensive, invasive, or targeted mechanisms dominate.
The result depends on the risk distribution and intervention effect.
claim: When risk is continuously distributed, most cases may arise from the large population at ordinary or moderately elevated risk rather than the small high-risk tail. Population-wide shifts can therefore produce more aggregate prevention even though each individual benefits only slightly.
interpretation: Aggregate benefit can conceal unequal burdens. Principia should report distributional effects and not use population averages to erase individual consent or subgroup harm.
